newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Piracy attacks up worldwide - maritime bureau.
newsitem.headline: Piracy attacks up worldwide - maritime bureau.

text.p: Pirate attacks on ships rose by five to a record 175 incidents worldwide in 1996, with Indonesia and Brazil the worst hit, the Regional Piracy Centre of the International Maritime Bureau said on Monday.
"There is no doubt that attacks on vessels have become more audacious, more violent and an issue of serious concern to shipping and seamen," the Kuala Lumpur-based centre said in its annual report.
The highest number of attacks was reported by Indonesia with 51 incidents in 1996 against 34 the previous year. Indonesia has seen a steady growth in such attacks since 1993, the piracy centre said.
Brazil was next with 15 cases of piracy last year.
Most of the attacks took place when ships were in port or anchored, the report said.
"The attacks in Brazil and many of the attacks in Indonesia have involved armed pirates and varying degrees of violence have been used," it said.
The report warned that Brazil could continue to suffer such violence as the country's authorities were indifferent to the problem.
"Brazil remains a highly dangerous area and this will continue to be so as long as the authorities fail to acknowledge the situation," it said.
The rise in incidents in 1996 came despite a drop in reported cases from ports in China, Hong Kong and Macau, which had seen a growing piracy problem over the last few years.
The report said the bureau was aware that ship masters have discouraged seamen from reporting pirate attacks.
"One reason for this may be the delay that the vessel may become subject to whilst all the reporting formalities are completed," it said.

In one of the bloodiest incidents last year, four armed pirates attacked a fishing boat off the Basilan islands in the Philippines and shot dead nine of the crew. One survivor escaped and reported it to police.

The report showed that incidents of ships being boarded increased to 124 in 1996 from 110 in 1995. Hijackings declined to five cases from 11 and the number of cases where vessels were fired upon fell to six from nine.
